title: 22 Eggshell waste as a substitute for limestone in beef cattle diets: A preliminary investigation
content:
Abstract
Limestone (LS), a nonrenewable resource, is a common source of Ca in animal feeds as it contains 95% calcium carbonate. Eggshell waste (ESW), which has a similar amount of calcium carbonate as LS, is an agricultural waste product from egg production that is currently being landfilled or incinerated. In 2018, 76.6 million tons of eggs were produced worldwide, with the U.S. as the second largest producer. In the U.S., egg processors spend $100,000 annually on ESW disposal, which is ranked as the 15th greatest agricultural pollutant. Repurposing ESW via economically sustainable applications could support a circular economy by reducing waste and benefiting multiple sectors. Research has been conducted to identify ways to add value to ESW, but use as cattle feed has not been evaluated. The objective of this study was to preliminarily analyze ESW as a substitute for LS as a Ca source in the diets of beef cattle consuming forage. These procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Texas State University (#9332). Three ruminally cannulated steers were used in a 3×3 Latin Square experiment and were randomly assigned one of three treatments that were mixed with cottonseed meal as a carrier: 1) no ESW or LS (CON), 2) ESW, and 3) LS where the experimental treatments were provided in iso-calcemic amounts at 0.37% of the previous 3-d dry matter intake. Each of the three 14-d periods included 8 d for treatment adaptation, 5 d for measurements of intake and digestion, and 1 d to collect rumen pH and blood samples. Treatment did not significantly affect forage organic matter intake (FOMI; P=0.60); FOMI for CON was 7.10 kg/d, for ESW was 7.22 kg/d, and for LS was 6.08 kg/d. Total digestible OM intake (TDOMI) was also not affected by treatment (P=0.41) and was 4.91 kg/d for CON, 4.50 kg/d for ESW, and 3.62 kg/d for LS. Dry matter digestibility (DMD) was not affected by treatment (P=0.82), ranging from 55.8% for ESW to 62.2% for CON. Organic matter digestibility (OMD) and NDF digestibility (NDFD) were also not affected by treatment (P≥0.12). These data, while preliminary, indicate that the substitution of ESW for LS as a Ca source did not significantly affect forage utilization in beef steers consuming forage. Data from our study could provide economic benefits to the egg production sector while also supporting environmental sustainability via diverting ESW from landfills into livestock feed as a replacement for LS. Future research should replicate these methods to confirm findings.
